entries.title: Where the podcast stands today
entries.summary: Real Choices…Real Life has 99 published episodes. The YouTube channel has 67 videos, 8 subscribers, 240 views in total and no playlists.
entries.body:
Real Choices…Real Life is the podcast of Abundance Legacy (ABL), the international nonprofit founded by Nathaniel X. Ross. It ran weekly on Buzzsprout from January 5, 2022 to January 17, 2024 and is listed on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Amazon Music and through its RSS feed.

No new episode has come out since January 2024. The catalog is finished, recorded and paid for, so the job now is not making content. It is getting existing content found.

The ABL YouTube channel (@AbundanceLegacyInc, joined October 29, 2022) showed 67 videos, 8 subscribers, 240 views in total and no playlists when checked on September 30, 2026. Most videos have fewer than 10 views. The channel’s About section already links to abundancelegacy.org, the podcast on Buzzsprout, and the podcast’s Instagram and Facebook.

details.Listed on: Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Amazon Music, RSS

entries.title: 99 episodes, 79 distinct shows
entries.summary: About one in five published episodes repeats an earlier recording. Upload each recording once.
entries.body:
Comparing titles and exact running times across all 99 episodes shows 79 distinct titles. Of the 20 repeated ones, 7 are exactly the same length as the original (a straight re-air) and 10 are exactly 1 minute 51 seconds longer (almost certainly the same recording with a new intro or outro). The last 3 share a title with an earlier episode but differ by a less regular amount, so someone needs to listen to the opening to be sure.

That matters for YouTube: uploading all 99 would put the same conversation on the channel twice, which splits views and looks careless. Upload one copy of each recording, preferably the later one if its extra 1:51 is a better intro.

The full catalog runs about 72.7 hours; the distinct recordings about 57.6 hours.

Eight episodes are already on YouTube as video recordings (see “What the 67 YouTube videos actually are”). Two of those videos, Holistic Living and Is Your Career Your Passion, match the later copy of a “listen to check” pair (#65 and #77) to the second, which suggests those later copies are separate recordings rather than repeats. So between 71 and 73 distinct recordings still need to go up; listening to #1 and #4 settles it.

entries.title: What listeners chose (April 2023 snapshot)
entries.summary: Per episode, Holistic Living and Finances drew the most downloads, even though Relationships had the most episodes.
entries.body:
The show’s own production file from April 2023 tracked downloads by theme. It is a snapshot of 47 sessions, not a current number, but it is the only audience data in hand.

Family and Relationships had the most episodes and the most downloads in total. Per episode, though, Holistic Living (about 25) and Finances (about 23) did best, then Spirituality (about 19), Career (about 18), Health (16) and Relationships (about 12). Almost all downloads came from the United States, with a handful from the UK, Canada, the Dominican Republic, Pakistan, Belgium and Jamaica.

So lead the YouTube relaunch with money and whole-life episodes, and treat Relationships as a deep library rather than the front door. Get fresh numbers from Buzzsprout’s Stats page before deciding anything big.

entries.title: Eight playlists for YouTube
entries.summary: Sort the 79 recordings by theme so viewers can binge a topic instead of scrolling a pile.
entries.body:
A channel with every video in one list gives a viewer no reason to watch the next one. Playlists named for what people are looking for keep them watching, and they tell YouTube what each video is about.

The show already named its themes, so the playlists follow them, plus two more: one for the holiday and year-end episodes, which suit giving season, and one for the episodes about Abundance Legacy itself, which every other video should point to at the end.

The old production file filed a few episodes oddly (a chiropractor episode under Career, for example). The sorting here goes by what each episode is actually about.

entries.title: Fix the channel before adding anything
entries.summary: Record the “before,” create the playlists, and sort the existing videos rather than deleting them.
entries.body:
Start by screen-recording the channel as it looks today and saving the numbers from YouTube Studio’s Analytics tab. That is the “before” that makes the pilot’s results believable.

The channel currently has no playlists at all, so every video sits in one long list. Create the eight podcast playlists, plus two more for what is already there: “It’s Your Life OWN It with Marissa” for the interview series, and “About Abundance Legacy” for the promos.

Don’t delete the 67 existing videos. People may have liked, saved or linked them, and deleting breaks those links. Instead, compare them against the 99-episode list, then either sort them into the new playlists or set true duplicates to Unlisted.

In Studio, open any video (the pencil icon) to edit its title, description and playlist; the Visibility column switches between Public, Unlisted and Private.

details.First: Screen-record the channel and save analytics
details.Old videos: Keep, sort or set to Unlisted
details.Playlists today: None — create 8 podcast + OWN It + About ABL

entries.title: Send the audio to YouTube through the RSS feed
entries.summary: YouTube can pull every Buzzsprout episode in automatically, as a video with the cover art as the picture.
entries.body:
This is the fastest way to put all 99 on YouTube, but it brings the repeats with it. The steps below were checked against Buzzsprout’s help pages in September 2026.

1. In Buzzsprout, go to Directories › Email Verification and add the email you use for YouTube, so YouTube can prove the feed is yours.
2. Turn off Buzzsprout Ads or any dynamic ad insertion — YouTube does not accept inserted ads. Ads read by the hosts inside the audio are fine.
3. Copy the feed address from Directories › RSS Feed.
4. In YouTube Studio, click Create, then New Podcast, then Submit RSS feed. Accept the terms and paste the address.
5. Enter the code YouTube emails to the feed’s address, then choose which episodes to bring in: all, those after a date, or only future ones.
6. YouTube takes a few days to process and imports everything as Private. When it is done, go to Content › Podcasts and click Publish under Video Count.

Tip: publishing brings the repeats too. Set the extra copies to Unlisted before you publish, or add episodes by hand instead.

details.Needs: Your email in the RSS feed; no inserted ads
details.Looks like: Cover art as a still picture with the audio

entries.title: If there are video recordings
entries.summary: Buzzsprout can now send real video straight to YouTube, but only on its video plan.
entries.body:
The how-to document in the handover says Buzzsprout cannot send video to YouTube. That was true once; it is out of date now. Buzzsprout’s Audio + Video plan (from $30 a month when checked in September 2026) connects a YouTube channel and publishes video episodes to YouTube, Apple Podcasts and Spotify, while the audio still goes everywhere else.

Nobody in the session could say where the original recordings live. Buzzsprout only hosts and distributes; the recording happened somewhere else. Ask the founder what he recorded with and where the files are before paying for a video plan. If only audio exists, the free RSS route above is the right one.

details.Open question: Where the original recordings are kept

entries.title: Ownership, credits and permission
entries.summary: Before anything is reused or monetized, get the founder to confirm in writing who owns what.
entries.body:
ABL produced the show, but guests brought their own words, faces and sometimes their own businesses. Reposting is one thing; cutting clips, selling access or asking for donations around someone’s appearance is another.

Get the founder to confirm, in writing, that ABL owns the recordings and may repost, edit and use them to raise money. For each guest, check whether they signed a release. Where nobody did, send a short, friendly note asking for a yes before their episode is cut into shorts.

Every description should credit who is on the episode by name and role. Never publish guests’ contact details: the old production file includes private emails and phone numbers, and those stay private.

details.Ask the founder: Does ABL own all recordings outright?
details.Guests: Signed release? If not, ask before clipping
details.Credit: Name and role in every description

entries.title: YouTube’s two license choices
entries.summary: Keep the Standard YouTube License. YouTube only offers that or CC BY, which lets anyone reuse the video.
entries.body:
In the session Ms. Lee remembered a license setting that let people share but not edit or earn from videos. That setting was on Vimeo, not YouTube. YouTube offers two choices only: the Standard YouTube License, which is the default, and Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY), which lets anyone reuse and edit the video as long as they credit you.

For ABL, keep Standard. Add a line to every description saying the content belongs to Abundance Legacy and may not be re-uploaded or edited without permission. It won’t stop a determined copier, but it states the terms plainly.

YouTube also checks each upload against its copyright-matching system, mostly for music, and warns you if it finds a match.

entries.title: Titles, descriptions and thumbnails
entries.summary: Most of the 67 videos have no real description. Each needs a clear title, who’s on it, and one next step.
entries.body:
People search for problems, not show names, so lead with the problem: “How to rebuild your credit” finds more people than “Understanding Your Credit | RCRL.”

A description that works: two sentences on what the viewer will learn; who is speaking, with name and role; one link to the free course or ABL’s giving page; the rights line; three to five hashtags people actually follow, such as #advocacy, #impact and #change.

Thumbnails: one face, three or four large words, and the playlist’s color, so the channel looks like one series. Write every description in fresh words rather than pasting the old Buzzsprout text.

Editing a title or description does not reset a video’s history. It won’t make an old video count as new, but a clearer title and thumbnail can lift how often YouTube shows it.

details.Title: Lead with the viewer’s problem
details.Description: What you’ll learn · who’s on it · one link · rights line · hashtags
details.Thumbnail: One face, 3–4 big words, playlist color

entries.title: The five-episode pilot
entries.summary: Do five episodes properly first, measure them, then show the founder the before and after.
entries.body:
Five recordings are already in ABL’s own storage: Holistic Living, Know Your Numbers, Finance 2023, Being a Health Advocate and Year End Wrap Part Two. They cover the two best-performing themes (whole-life and money), a guest episode and a year-end episode that fits giving season.

For each one: a new problem-first title, a fresh description with credits and one link, a thumbnail, the right playlist, and two or three shorts. Then leave them for a week and compare views, watch time and new subscribers with the “before” you recorded.

The file names don’t say which copy of a repeated episode they came from; play the first minute to confirm before titling.

details.Episodes: Holistic Living · Know Your Numbers · Finance 2023 · Being a Health Advocate · Year End Wrap Part Two

entries.title: A daily rhythm: long episodes plus shorts
entries.summary: Three full episodes a day, each cut into shorts, clears the catalog in about four weeks.
entries.body:
Every episode runs 30 minutes to an hour. That is right for people who already care, but strangers find a channel through short clips. Each long episode should give two or three shorts: a strong opinion, a practical tip or a moment of emotion, each under a minute, with large captions and the ABL name on screen.

A pace one person can keep: prepare three long episodes a day and their shorts, schedule them rather than posting live, and keep a steady time each day. Ms. Lee’s target in the session was five to ten a day; start at three and raise it once the routine is quick.

At three a day, the 79 distinct recordings take about 27 working days. YouTube Studio can schedule uploads for a set time, so the work can be done in batches.

entries.title: What YouTube will and won’t pay
entries.summary: Ad money is a long way off, and the bar doubles in February 2027. Plan to raise money through ABL instead.
entries.body:
YouTube’s first earning tier needs 500 subscribers, three public uploads in the last 90 days, and either 3,000 watch hours in a year or 3 million Shorts views in 90 days. It unlocks memberships, Super Thanks and similar tips, not ad money.

Ad money needs 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 watch hours in a year (or 10 million Shorts views in 90 days). From February 1, 2027, new applicants will need 8,000 watch hours or 20 million Shorts views instead.

With 8 subscribers, that is years away. The channel’s real job is to introduce people to ABL and lead them to the course and to giving. Treat any YouTube money as a bonus.

details.First tier: 500 subs + 3 uploads/90 days + 3,000 hrs or 3M Shorts views

entries.title: Monthly support through Buzzsprout
entries.summary: Buzzsprout can take monthly gifts from listeners and keeps 15%. It needs a paid plan.
entries.body:
Buzzsprout has two ways to take money: Listener Support (monthly contributions) and Subscriptions (paid extras such as bonus or early episodes). Both need a paid Buzzsprout plan. Buzzsprout keeps 15% and ABL keeps 85%, paid into a Buzzsprout wallet that can be spent on the plan or cashed out through PayPal.

The founder has said he wants the episodes to stay free, so Listener Support fits better than paid extras. Before switching it on, read the terms and decide who at ABL handles the PayPal account and the reporting that comes with taking money for a nonprofit.

The supporter list can be exported as a spreadsheet, which is how those names reach ABL’s own newsletter.

entries.title: From a video to a gift
entries.summary: Every video should point to one place: the free course, which ends with an invitation to give.
entries.body:
The founder’s course is free. At the end he asks people who found it useful to donate. That is the funnel: a short clip catches someone, a full episode earns trust, one link takes them to the course sign-up, and the course ends with the ask.

Keep it to one link per video, always the same one, so results are easy to measure. The “About Abundance Legacy” episodes become the end-screen for every other video, so a viewer who liked a money episode learns who made it.

What to watch weekly: clicks on the link (YouTube Studio shows them), course sign-ups, and gifts. If sign-ups rise, the channel is working even before the numbers look big.

ABL already has these destinations on abundancelegacy.org: the Financial Boot Camp, life coaching, support groups, an email sign-up and a donate page. Match the link to the episode: money episodes to the Boot Camp, relationship episodes to coaching or support groups.

details.Step 3: One link to the free course
details.Step 4: The course ends with an invitation to give
details.Ready-made links: Boot Camp · Coaching · Support groups · Email list · Donate

entries.title: Giving season
entries.summary: Nonprofits raise much of their year between Thanksgiving and December 31. The pilot should be live before then.
entries.body:
GivingTuesday 2026 falls on December 1, the Tuesday after Thanksgiving. The show already has Thanksgiving, Christmas and year-end episodes that suit this stretch.

A simple plan: have the pilot live and the first two playlists filled by mid-November; re-release the Thanksgiving and year-end episodes with fresh titles in the weeks before; on GivingTuesday, post one short where the founder says in his own words what a gift makes possible, linking to ABL’s giving page.

Keep claims honest. Only describe impact ABL can show.

entries.title: Keep the people who already came
entries.summary: The few people already subscribed are the easiest to reach. Turn them into a list ABL owns.
entries.body:
Platforms can change their rules overnight; an email list belongs to ABL. Gather the people who already follow the show: Buzzsprout supporter exports, the YouTube subscribers, and the Instagram and Facebook followers.

Send a short, regular newsletter: the new episode or playlist, one line about what ABL did that month, and the course link. Reminding people what the organization does is how giving starts.

Ms. Lee’s own experience in the session: posting steadily with hashtags people follow (advocacy, impact, change) brought opportunities to her within weeks. Add personal outreach — about ten friendly messages a day to people who comment or follow — and it compounds.

entries.title: Hosting the audio in ABL’s own storage
entries.summary: Keeping copies in ABL’s own storage gives control and a backup, but public links can be downloaded by anyone.
entries.body:
The five pilot episodes already sit in ABL’s Supabase storage. Holding the full set there means ABL keeps a copy that does not depend on any one platform, and the files can feed ABL’s own site or course.

Two cautions. A public storage bucket means anyone with the link can download the file — the same as Buzzsprout’s download button today, but worth knowing. And storage and bandwidth cost money past a plan’s free limits, so check the Supabase plan before moving 99 files there.

Moving files does not take them off Buzzsprout; Buzzsprout stays the source for podcast apps.

details.Now: 5 pilot files in ABL’s Supabase storage
details.Check first: Storage & bandwidth limits of the plan

entries.title: Pricing Ms. Lee’s work
entries.summary: Price in batches of five, lead with the pilot as proof, and agree what “done” means per episode.
entries.body:
Putting 99 videos online is a different job from relaunching them. The work that earns a fee is the relaunch: sorting, retitling, rewriting descriptions, thumbnails, shorts and measuring results.

Offer it as batches of five episodes at a set price, with the pilot as the first batch. Write down exactly what each batch includes, so the founder sees what he is paying for and can stop or continue after any batch. Ms. Lee sets the price.

Show progress in the founder’s own terms: a screen recording before, the same view after, and the analytics side by side.

details.Each batch includes: Titles, descriptions, thumbnails, playlists, shorts, a results note

entries.title: How Ms. Lee works
entries.summary: Storytelling first, short sprints, quick replies and real relationships instead of paid ads.
entries.body:
Ms. Lee is a global consultant whose background runs from finance and pharmaceuticals in South Africa to consulting across continents. Her own studio’s plan describes the approach this agent follows: tell the story before selling anything, work in short sprints of two to six weeks, reply within a day or two, and build through gatherings, partnerships and steady posting rather than paid ads.

For ABL that means: lead with the founder’s mission and the people on the show, prove results on a small batch before asking for more, and keep every step measurable.

details.Growth: Relationships and steady posting, not paid ads

entries.title: Questions for the founder
entries.summary: Eight answers unlock the rest of the plan.
entries.body:
1. Does ABL own every recording outright, and may it edit, clip and raise money around them?
2. Did guests sign releases? If not, may we ask them now?
3. Eight 2022 episodes are already on YouTube as video. Do video recordings exist for the other episodes, and where are the original files?
4. Is there written agreement between you and whoever managed the channel before?
5. Which link should every video point to: the course sign-up or the giving page?
6. Who handles donations and the reporting that comes with them?
7. Which of the three episodes that share a title but not a length (Holistic Living, Is Your Career Your Passion?, Finance 2023) are new recordings?
8. The YouTube channel also carries about 51 “It’s Your Life OWN It” videos with Marissa. Is that series part of this relaunch, and does ABL have the rights to reuse it?

entries.title: Rules for everything published
entries.summary: Credit people, protect their privacy, label AI edits and never invent results.
entries.body: Credit everyone by name and role. Never publish guests’ personal contact details. Don’t invent testimonials, numbers or quotes; if a result isn’t measured, don’t claim it. When a video uses AI to change someone’s face or voice, YouTube asks creators to disclose realistic altered content, so tick that box. Keep the Standard license. Don’t delete old videos without checking what links to them. And treat second-hand claims about what TikTok or Facebook pay creators as rumours until checked.

entries.title: What the 67 YouTube videos actually are
entries.summary: Only 8 are podcast episodes. Most of the channel is a different show, plus 8 short promos.
entries.body:
Reading the channel’s Videos tab on September 30, 2026:

1. 8 are podcast episodes recorded on video in 2022, with Nathaniel X. Ross, Jessica Karin and Stephanie Jackson: Health & Relationships, Discovering Your Spirituality, Understanding Energy 1, Am I Doing What I Love, Do I Have The Right Relationship, Holistic Living, Is Your Career Your Passion, and Cleaning Up Your Inner Circle. Their lengths match the podcast episodes to within seconds.
2. 8 are short promos under two minutes: Real Choices Real Life Podcast Commercial, Women Group Commercial, Men’s Group Commercial, Hump Revised Video 2, Donation Video, Article Video, Financial Boot Camp Commercial and Choice Video.
3. The other 51 or so are a separate interview show, “Nathaniel X. Ross on It’s Your Life OWN It — Motivational Moments with Marissa,” with Marissa Bloedoorn of OWN It! Magazine & Publishing and guests such as Jacqueline Lulu Brown, Coach Tiffany Parra, Elaine Scales and Dr. Stephanie Reid. Several share the same thumbnail and length, so some are probably uploaded more than once.

What this means: almost none of the podcast is on YouTube yet. Upload the remaining 71 to 73 distinct recordings (see the catalog section for why the range), and treat the OWN It videos as their own series with their own playlist instead of mixing them into the podcast playlists. The OWN It count is by subtraction (67 minus 16), and the possible repeats need checking in YouTube Studio, where every video’s exact title, date and length are listed under Content.

entries.title: What Abundance Legacy offers
entries.summary: Podcast, Financial Boot Camp, life coaching, support groups and articles, plus volunteering, an email list and online giving.
entries.body:
From abundancelegacy.org (checked September 30, 2026): the vision is to help people become critical thinkers who make healthy decisions in their lives and relationships. Programs listed are the podcast, a Financial Boot Camp (a one-month program meeting once a week for two hours by video), life coaching, support groups and articles. The site invites people to volunteer, learn (podcast, articles, calendar) and donate, and has an email sign-up in the footer.

That gives every video a real next step: money episodes can point to the Financial Boot Camp, relationship and family episodes to life coaching or support groups, and everything else to the email list or the donate page. The site already has testimonial videos; reuse those rather than writing new ones.

details.Programs: Podcast · Financial Boot Camp · Life Coaching · Support Groups · Articles
